title: Same fitness, different costs for females and males: a commentary on ‘Diverging sex ratios in dioecious Proteaceae are exacerbated by anthropogenic disruptions to the fire cycle’
content: Every offspring has both a mother and a father and this simple fact constrains the average fitness of females and males to be equal (Fisher, 1930). In plants, this identity applies strictly to dioecious species (separate female and male plants; ∼7 % of angiosperms; Renner, 2014), but it generalizes to all flowering plants: all zygotes arise from fusion of an egg and a sperm. Lifetime fitness emerges from successive reproductive allocations, each contributing positively to total reproductive success. However, these allocations also trade off against future reproduction through reduced survival, growth or fecundity (Williams, 1966). These fitness-based trade-offs define the costs of reproduction (Dorken et al., 2025). For dioecious plants, where fitness is partitioned between distinct female and male individuals, this raises a natural question: if mean lifetime fitness must be equal between the sexes, must their mean lifetime reproductive costs also be equal?
